tools.name: Hook analyzer

plans.name: Starter
plans.who: For creators posting a few times a week

steps.title: Add your video
steps.body: Upload a file or paste a TikTok, Reels or Shorts link. Hooks and scripts work as plain text.

steps.title: Swipeproof reviews it
steps.body: It checks the opening, pacing, format and the ask at the end.

steps.title: Read your score
steps.body: One number from 0 to 100, with a score for each area behind it.

steps.title: Fix and re-check
steps.body: Every finding has a timecode and a specific change. Edit, then run it again.

samples.prob: The opening greets the audience before anything happens.
samples.fix: Open on the finished result, then explain how you got there.

samples.prob: One sentence runs 31 words with no visual change.
samples.fix: Split it into two beats and cut to a new angle between them.

samples.prob: The video stops without asking for anything.
samples.fix: Close with one ask, such as a question viewers can answer in a comment.

faq.a: No. Each finding quotes a timecode or a line from what you submitted, and the fix refers to that moment. If a rule does not apply to your video it does not appear.

faq.q: What if a finding is wrong?
faq.a: Treat the score as a second opinion. Each area shows why it scored the way it did, so you can ignore one you disagree with and re-run after edits.

faq.q: Does it work for my niche?
faq.a: The checks cover structure: how fast the opening lands, how long each beat runs, whether the format fits a vertical feed. Those apply to tutorials, clips, product videos and talking-head content alike.

faq.q: I already see my retention graph. Why use this?
faq.a: A retention graph shows where people left after you posted. Swipeproof points at likely weak moments before you post and suggests a change for each one.
In this demo, uploaded files are read inside your browser and never sent anywhere. Reports are saved only in this browser.

faq.q: Can I try it without paying?
faq.a: Yes. All three tools run without an account. Paid plans in this demo are placeholders and no payment is taken.

platforms.name: TikTok
platforms.line: Built for a feed where the next video is one flick away.

tips.title: Lead with the payoff
tips.body: Show the result in the first second. Context can follow once people have a reason to stay.

tips.title: Keep text clear of the edges
tips.body: Buttons sit on the right and the caption sits at the bottom, so place on-screen text in the upper middle.

tips.title: Write for sound off and sound on
tips.body: Add captions for silent viewers and keep the first spoken line short for everyone else.

platforms.name: Instagram Reels
platforms.line: Built for a grid, a feed and a Reels tab at once.

tips.title: Pick a cover that reads small
tips.body: The cover shows in your profile grid, so choose a frame with one clear subject and few words.

tips.title: Make the first frame a still worth pausing on
tips.body: Reels autoplay in the main feed next to photos, so the opening frame has to hold up as an image.

tips.title: Give people a reason to send it
tips.body: End with something a viewer would forward to a friend, such as a checklist or a single surprising fact.

platforms.name: YouTube Shorts
platforms.line: Built for viewers who also search.

tips.title: Say the topic out loud early
tips.body: A plain statement of the topic in the first line helps the right viewers recognize the video is for them.

tips.title: Title it like an answer
tips.body: Write the title as the phrase someone would type, then deliver that answer in the video.

tips.title: Point to the longer video
tips.body: If the Short comes from a longer upload, tell viewers where the full version lives.

posts.title: What the first three seconds have to do
posts.excerpt: An opening has three jobs. Most weak hooks skip the second one.
body: An opening line has three jobs: stop the thumb, name the topic and promise something. Greetings do none of them, which is why a hello costs you viewers before the video has started.
The job people skip most is naming the topic. A dramatic line with no subject makes viewers curious for half a second, then they leave because they cannot tell whether the video is for them.
A quick test: read only your first sentence to someone. If they can tell you what the video is about and what they will get from it, the hook is doing its work.

posts.title: How to find the line where viewers leave
posts.excerpt: Drop-offs cluster around a few predictable moments. Here is where to look first.
body: Viewers rarely leave at random. They leave when a sentence runs long, when the picture has not changed for a while, or when you start explaining before showing.
Read your script aloud with a timer. Mark any sentence that takes more than about eight seconds to say. Those are the first candidates to split or cut.
Then look at the footage over the same lines. If the frame is identical for that whole stretch, add a cut, a zoom or an on-screen label so the eye has something new.

posts.title: Write scripts in beats
posts.excerpt: A beat is one idea you can say in a breath. Scripts built from beats are easier to edit.
body: A beat is a single idea you can say in one breath, usually under fifteen words. Writing in beats forces each line to earn its place.
Lay the beats out as a list. The first is the hook, the second says what the viewer will get, the middle ones deliver it and the last one asks for something.
When a video feels slow, you can now see why. Either a beat is carrying two ideas or two beats are saying the same thing.

posts.title: End on one ask
posts.excerpt: Three calls to action get less response than one. Pick the one that fits the video.
body: Asking viewers to like, follow, comment and share in one breath gives them four things to ignore. One ask gets more response than several.
Match the ask to the video. A tutorial earns a save. An opinion earns a comment. A funny clip earns a share.
Put the ask after the payoff. If it arrives before the viewer has what they came for, it reads as a toll.

posts.title: Captions people can read at a glance
posts.excerpt: Caption problems are usually timing problems. A few rules cover most of them.
body: Most caption problems come from timing. Text that appears for less than a second and a half is gone before most people finish reading it.
Keep each caption to a short phrase and keep it away from the edges of the frame, where app buttons and descriptions cover it.
Contrast matters more than font choice. Light text needs a dark backing and dark text needs a light one, because the footage behind it keeps changing.

posts.title: Cutting long videos into shorts that stand alone
posts.excerpt: A clip lifted from a longer video needs its own opening and its own ending.
body: A good moment inside a long video depends on what came before it. Lifted out on its own, it often starts mid-thought.
Give each clip a new first line that states the topic. One sentence recorded after the fact or a text label on screen is enough.
Reframe for vertical as well. A wide two-person shot becomes two small faces on a phone, so crop to whoever is speaking.

posts.title: Frame for vertical first
posts.excerpt: Shooting wide and cropping later loses resolution and composition. Plan the tall frame.
body: If a video is headed for a phone feed, compose it tall from the start. Cropping a wide shot throws away most of the pixels and usually cuts off something that mattered.
Put the subject in the middle third of the frame and leave room above and below for text.
Check the export too. A vertical frame at 1080 by 1920 keeps text and faces sharp on current phones.
